usage: Time particle 에 marks the day an event happens; this is the form you reach for most.
부터 marks the starting point of a stretch of time (vs 까지 for the end).
Korean prefers 다음 주 월요일 (next week's Monday); bare 다음 월요일 sounds incomplete.
The day comes first, then the time-of-day word: 월요일 아침, 월요일 저녁.
examples: 오늘은 월요일이에요.
Today is Monday.
이에요 simply states what day it is; 오늘 (today) needs no 에.
월요일에 학교에 가요.
I go to school on Monday.
Both 월요일 (when) and 학교 (where) take 에 — 에 covers time and destination.
월요일부터 다시 바빠질 것 같아요.
It looks like I'll get busy again from Monday.
Real-life grumble: 부터 sets the day the busy stretch starts.
nuance: 월요일 is the start of the Korean work and school week, just as in English, and it carries the same slightly heavy 'back to the grind' feeling captured in 월요병 ('Monday sickness,' the Monday blues). It is Sino-Korean: 月 (moon/month) + 曜 (the celestial-body element shared by all weekday names) + 日 (day) — the seven days are literally named after the moon, fire, water, wood, metal, earth, and sun. The single biggest English-speaker pitfall is the preposition: English 'on Monday' makes you want a word, but Korean glues the time particle 에 to the noun (월요일에), and dropping it (월요일 가요) sounds broken. Note also that days are NOT capitalized concepts in Korean and never take a plural — '월요일은' with topic 은 is how you say 'Mondays (as a rule)'.

mistakes: Saying '월요일 가요' without the particle. A specific day of the week needs the time marker, so it must be 월요일에 가요.
Writing it as two words '월 요일'. It is one fused noun, 월요일, with no space.
Saying '다음 월요일' for 'next Monday'. Koreans normally say 다음 주 월요일 (next week's Monday).

usage: Attach 에 to state the day something is scheduled.
까지 marks an end point or deadline (the partner of 부터).
Pair the day with 지난주 to point back into the past week.
매주 ('every week') + the day expresses a weekly routine.
examples: 내일은 화요일이에요.
Tomorrow is Tuesday.
이에요 states the day; 내일 (tomorrow) takes no 에.
화요일에 약속이 있어요.
I have plans on Tuesday.
약속 here means a set appointment with someone, very common with days.
매주 화요일마다 한국어 수업이 있어요.
I have Korean class every Tuesday.
마다 ('each') stacks with 매주 화요일 to stress a recurring slot.
nuance: 화요일 is the second day of the week, the day after 월요일. The 화 is Sino-Korean 火 'fire' (the same 화 in 화산 'volcano' and 화재 'fire/blaze'), following the East Asian seven-luminaries naming system; you don't need the hanja to use the word, but knowing it helps you keep the order straight. Learners most often confuse 화요일 (Tuesday) with 수요일 (Wednesday) and 토요일 (Saturday) because the syllables 화/수/토 look short and similar — anchor them by their hanja meanings (fire/water/earth). As with every weekday, English speakers tend to omit the particle; 'on Tuesday' must become 화요일에, and 'until Tuesday' is 화요일까지, not a separate preposition word.

As with every weekday, English speakers tend to omit the particle; 'on Tuesday' must become 화요일에, and 'until Tuesday' is 화요일까지, not a separate preposition word.

mistakes: Confusing 화요일 (Tuesday) with 수요일 (Wednesday). Remember the fixed order: 화 (fire) comes before 수 (water).
Dropping the particle: it should be 화요일에 와요, not 화요일 와요.
Saying '화요일에까지'. Stack only one particle — for a deadline it is just 화요일까지.

usage: 에 marks the day of the event — the default form.
Day first, then 오후 (afternoon); good for pinning down a meeting time.
이번 주 + the day specifies which Wednesday you mean.
쯤 ('about') softens it to an approximate day.
examples: 오늘이 수요일이에요?
Is today Wednesday?
이에요? turns it into a question; subject 이 (오늘이) checks the fact.
수요일에 시간 있어요?
Do you have time on Wednesday?
A natural way to propose meeting; 시간 있어요? = 'are you free?'
수요일쯤에 다시 연락할게요.
I'll get in touch again around Wednesday.
쯤 + 에 keeps the day vague; 연락할게요 promises future action.
nuance: 수요일 sits in the middle of the work week, between 화요일 and 목요일, so it often feels like the 'hump' or halfway mark of a busy week. The 수 is Sino-Korean 水 'water' (the same 수 in 수영 'swimming' and 홍수 'flood'), part of the fixed fire-water-wood-metal-earth ordering of the weekday names. Because 수요일 and 목요일 both start with quiet single syllables, beginners swap them — lock 수 (water) before 목 (wood). The classic English-speaker error is using the wrong particle: to say 'on Wednesday' you mark time with 에 (수요일에), never the subject marker, so '수요일이 있어요' (literally 'Wednesday exists') is wrong for 'there is something on Wednesday' — that is 수요일에 있어요.

mistakes: Mixing up 수요일 (Wed) and 목요일 (Thu). The fixed order is 수 (water) before 목 (wood).
Saying '수요일이 있어요' to mean 'on Wednesday'. The time marker is 에, so it is 수요일에 있어요.
Treating 수요일 as a verb-like word; it is a plain noun, so events attach with 에, not by conjugating the day.

usage: 에 marks when the event happens.
Day + 저녁; 저녁 covers both 'evening' and the evening meal.
Use 다음 주 목요일 rather than bare 다음 목요일.
까지 sets Thursday as the deadline.
examples: 모레가 목요일이에요.
The day after tomorrow is Thursday.
모레가 ... 이에요 identifies the day; no 에 on 모레.
목요일에 친구를 만나요.
I'm meeting a friend on Thursday.
만나다 takes the object marker 를 (친구를) — you meet a person, not 'with' one here.
목요일까지 보고서를 끝내야 해요.
I have to finish the report by Thursday.
Workplace reality: 까지 = the hard deadline, 해야 해요 = obligation.
nuance: 목요일 is the fourth day of the week, right before 금요일, and people often start eyeing the weekend from here (the cheerful '불목' — 'fire Thursday,' a night out — plays on this). It is Sino-Korean 木 'wood/tree' (the same 목 in 목재 'lumber'; note it is a different 목 from 目 'eye' or 목 'neck' — context and the 요일 ending keep it clear). Learners confuse 목요일 (Thu) with 금요일 (Fri); fix the order as 목 (wood) before 금 (metal/gold). A frequent English-speaker slip is with 만나다: English says 'meet WITH a friend,' but Korean treats the person as a direct object, so it is 친구를 만나요, and the day still needs its own particle, 목요일에.

Forgetting the particle: it is 목요일에 만나요, not 목요일 만나요.
Saying '친구하고 만나요' and then '친구를 만나요' interchangeably and getting the particle wrong; the plain 'meet someone' pattern is 친구를 만나다.

usage: 에 marks when; the most common form.
Day + 밤; 금요일 밤 is the prime time for going out.
이번 주 + the day pins down which Friday.
Slang clipping of 불타는 금요일 ('burning Friday'); casual speech only.
examples: 오늘은 금요일이에요.
Today is Friday.
이에요 states the day; the topic 은 frames 오늘.
금요일에 영화를 봐요.
I'm watching a movie on Friday.
보다 here means 'watch'; 영화를 보다 is the set collocation for seeing a film.
드디어 금요일이네요! 오늘은 불금이에요.
Finally Friday! Today's a wild Friday.
드디어 ('finally') + ~네요 (realization) capture the relief; 불금 is friendly slang.
nuance: 금요일 is the last workday before the weekend, so it carries a light, celebratory mood — Koreans cheer 불금 (from 불타는 금요일, 'burning Friday') the way English says TGIF, but keep that slang for friends, not your boss. The 금 is Sino-Korean 金 'metal/gold' (the same 금 in 금메달 'gold medal' and 황금 'gold'), continuing the fixed weekday order. Watch a film/movie is 영화를 보다, where 보다 means 'watch/see' — don't reach for an English-style 'look at.' The recurring English-speaker mistake stays the same: 'on Friday' is 금요일에, never a bare 금요일 before the verb, and 'this Friday' is more naturally 이번 주 금요일 than 이번 금요일.

mistakes: Confusing 금요일 (Fri) with 토요일 (Sat). Keep the order 금 (metal) before 토 (earth).
Saying '금요일 봐요' without the particle. The natural form is 금요일에 봐요.
Using 불금 in formal or work settings. It is casual slang; in polite contexts just say 금요일.

usage: Day + 아침; 아침 also means breakfast, so context decides.
이번 주 + the day to specify which Saturday.
하고 ('and') links the two weekend days in speech.
examples: 내일은 토요일이에요.
Tomorrow is Saturday.
이에요 states the day; 내일 needs no 에.
토요일에 집에서 쉬어요.
I rest at home on Saturday.
Place uses 에서 (집에서) for an action's location, while the day uses 에.
토요일은 보통 늦잠을 자요.
On Saturdays I usually sleep in.
Topic 은 = 'as for Saturdays'; 늦잠을 자다 is the set phrase for sleeping late.
nuance: 토요일 is the first day of the Korean weekend (주말 = Saturday + Sunday), so most people are off work or school and it reads as a relaxed, do-something day. The 토 is Sino-Korean 土 'earth/soil' (the same 토 in 토지 'land' and 영토 'territory'), the sixth of the seven luminaries. A subtle trap here is that the DAY of an action takes 에 (토요일에) but the PLACE of the action takes 에서 (집에서 쉬어요) — English 'at home on Saturday' uses one preposition each, but Korean splits time vs. dynamic location across two particles. Beginners also mix 토요일 (Sat) with 일요일 (Sun); fix it as 토 (earth) before 일 (sun).

mistakes: Mixing up 토요일 (Sat) and 일요일 (Sun). The order is 토 (earth) before 일 (sun).
Dropping the particle: it should be 토요일에 쉬어요, not 토요일 쉬어요.
Using 에 for the place of an action: rest happens 집에서, not 집에 — 'rest at home' is 집에서 쉬어요.

usage: 오전 (a.m./forenoon) is the clock-based partner of 오후 (p.m.).
이번 주 + the day to make clear which Sunday.
마다 ('each') turns the day into a weekly habit.
examples: 오늘이 일요일이에요?
Is today Sunday?
이에요? asks; subject 이 (오늘이) checks the fact of the day.
일요일에 교회에 가요.
I go to church on Sunday.
교회 takes 에 as a destination — same particle as the day, different role.
일요일마다 가족하고 시간을 보내요.
I spend time with my family every Sunday.
가족하고 = 'with family'; 시간을 보내다 is the set phrase 'spend time.'
nuance: 일요일 is the last day of the weekend, a rest-and-recharge day before the new week, and on most Korean calendars it sits in the first column printed in red as a public holiday. The 일 is Sino-Korean 日 'sun/day' (the same 日 that ends every weekday name and appears in 일기 'diary'), so 일요일 literally reads 'sun-day' — a neat parallel to English. Don't confuse the standalone word 요일, which only means 'day of the week' (used in the question 무슨 요일이에요? 'what day is it?'), with 일요일 'Sunday'. As always for English speakers, 'on Sunday' is 일요일에, and 'spend time WITH family' is 가족하고/가족과 시간을 보내요, where 하고 carries the 'with.'

Saying '일요일 가요' without the particle. Use 일요일에 가요.
Forgetting the 'with' particle: it is 가족하고 시간을 보내요, not 가족 시간을 보내요.

usage: 에 marks the day off when something happens (or doesn't).
이라서 ('because it is') gives the reason offices are closed.
법정 ('legally fixed') stresses it is an official, mandated day off.
대체 ('replacement') — a make-up day off when a holiday falls on a weekend.
examples: 내일은 공휴일이에요.
Tomorrow is a public holiday.
이에요 states the fact; 내일 needs no 에.
공휴일에는 은행이 문을 닫아요.
On public holidays, banks are closed.
에는 = 에 + 는, adding a 'as for that day' contrast; 문을 닫다 = 'close (shop).'
오늘은 공휴일이라서 학교에 안 가요.
Today is a holiday, so I don't go to school.
이라서 links cause to result; 안 가요 negates the verb.
nuance: 공휴일 is an official, calendar-fixed day off when offices, banks, schools, and public services close for everyone at once — think 설날 (Lunar New Year) or 추석 (Chuseok). It is fully Sino-Korean: 公 'public' + 休 'rest' + 日 'day,' literally 'public rest day.' The key contrast for learners is 공휴일 vs. 휴가: 휴가 (休暇) is YOUR personal leave/vacation that you request and take individually, whereas 공휴일 is a national day off no one schedules. Also distinguish 휴일 (any non-work day, including weekends) from 공휴일 (specifically an official public holiday). The usual English-speaker pitfall returns with the particle — 'on a holiday' is 공휴일에 (often 공휴일에는 for contrast), and 'closed' is the idiom 문을 닫다, not a literal translation of 'be closed.'

Saying '공휴일 닫아요' without the particle. Use 공휴일에 닫아요 (or 공휴일에는).
Translating 'is closed' word for word. Korean says 문을 닫아요 ('closes its door'), not a passive 'be closed.'

usage: Add 에 to mark the time frame of an event.
이번 + 주말 (weekend); note 주말 is one word.
이번 주 + a specific day narrows it down.
all this week / the whole week
examples: 이번 주에 시험이 있어요.
I have an exam this week.
이번 주 + 에 sets the time; 시험이 있다 = 'there is an exam.'
이번 주는 너무 바빠요.
This week is so busy.
Topic 는 frames the week; 바쁘다 is a descriptive verb (adjective), so no object.
이번 주말에 시간 괜찮으면 같이 밥 먹어요.
If you're free this weekend, let's eat together.
이번 주말에 + a soft invitation; 밥 먹다 ('eat a meal') doubles as 'grab food.'
nuance: 이번 주 means the week we are currently in, the now-frame for plans and schedules. 이번 is native-Korean-style 'this (time/occasion)' and 주 is Sino-Korean 週 'week,' so the phrase is a hybrid 'this week.' It belongs to a tidy set: 지난주 (last week), 이번 주 (this week), 다음 주 (next week). The spacing trips up nearly every learner: 이번 주 and 다음 주 are written as TWO words (a space before 주), but 지난주 is fused into ONE word — a real inconsistency you simply memorize. As with all time nouns, 'this week' as a when-phrase takes 에 (이번 주에), and note that 바쁘다 ('busy') is an adjective-type verb, so you say 이번 주는 바빠요, never add an object to it.

mistakes: Writing 이번주 as one word. The standard spelling is 이번 주 with a space before 주.
Forgetting the particle: say 이번 주에 있어요, not 이번 주 있어요.
Mismatching the set: 지난주 is one word but 이번 주 / 다음 주 take a space — don't apply one rule to all three.

usage: Add 에 to mark the future time frame.
다음 + 주말 (weekend), written as one word 주말.
다음 주 + a specific day — the natural way to say 'next Monday.'
examples: 다음 주에 여행을 가요.
I'm going on a trip next week.
다음 주 + 에 sets future time; 여행을 가다 = 'go on a trip.'
다음 주는 좀 한가해요.
Next week is a bit free.
Topic 는 frames the week; 한가하다 ('be free/relaxed') is descriptive.
다음 주 월요일에 다시 회의하기로 했어요.
We decided to meet again next Monday.
다음 주 월요일에 + ~기로 하다 ('decide to') for a settled plan.
nuance: 다음 주 means the week that follows this one, so it naturally pairs with future plans and future-leaning verbs. 다음 ('next') + 주 (週 'week') mirrors the structure of 이번 주, and the trio 지난주 / 이번 주 / 다음 주 should be learned together. The contrast to watch is 다음 ('next in a sequence') versus 내년·내일 style words: for weeks you use 다음 주, not a single fused word, and 'next Monday' is idiomatically 다음 주 월요일, not 다음 월요일. Spacing again matters — 다음 주 takes a space like 이번 주, while only 지난주 is written solid. And the time particle holds: a when-phrase is 다음 주에, so 'I'm going next week' is 다음 주에 가요, never bare 다음 주 가요.

usage: Add 에 to mark when; almost always with past tense.
Here 지난 + 주말 takes a space (지난 주말), unlike solid 지난주.
지난주 + a specific day points back into the past week.
내내 ('throughout') stresses the whole past span.
examples: 지난주에 부산에 갔어요.
I went to Busan last week.
지난주 + 에 with past 갔어요 — 지난주 forces past tense.
지난주는 정말 힘들었어요.
Last week was really hard.
Topic 는 frames it; 힘들다 ('be tough') in past 힘들었어요.
지난주 금요일에 친구를 만났어요.
I met a friend last Friday.
지난주 금요일에 + past 만났어요; 친구를 만나다 takes object 를.
nuance: 지난주 means the week that just ended, so it lives in the past and pulls past-tense verbs with it (갔어요, 만났어요). 지난 is the adnominal form of 지나다 'to pass,' literally 'the week that has passed,' and 주 is 週 'week.' It is the past member of the set 지난주 / 이번 주 / 다음 주. The most notorious detail is spacing: 지난주 ('last week') is written as ONE word, but 이번 주 and 다음 주 take a space — and confusingly, 지난 주말 ('last weekend') splits back into two words because 주말 is its own noun. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: keep the time particle (지난주에) and don't use present tense — 'I went last week' must be 지난주에 갔어요, not 지난주에 가요.

usage: A pure adverbial time word; usually stands alone with no particle.
까지 attaches for a deadline (one of the few particles 모레 takes).
the morning of the day after tomorrow
모레 + 아침 stacks the time-of-day after the day word.
When 모레 is the subject of an 'is' sentence, use 가: 모레가 토요일이에요.
examples: 모레 시험이 있어요.
I have an exam the day after tomorrow.
모레 sits bare as the time; no 에 needed.
모레가 토요일이에요.
The day after tomorrow is Saturday.
Here 모레 is the subject, so it takes 가, then 이에요 names the day.
모레까지 숙제를 꼭 내야 해요.
I absolutely have to hand in the homework by the day after tomorrow.
모레까지 = the deadline; 꼭 ('for sure') + 내야 해요 stresses obligation.
nuance: 모레 means two days from today, one step past 내일 (tomorrow): the sequence runs 어제 (yesterday) → 오늘 (today) → 내일 (tomorrow) → 모레 → 글피 (three days out). Unlike the Sino-Korean day-of-week names, 모레 is a native Korean word and a bare time adverb. The crucial English-speaker pitfall is the particle: relative time words like 모레, 내일, 오늘, 어제 normally take NO 에 — 'I'll meet you the day after tomorrow' is 모레 만나요, and adding 에 (모레에) sounds wrong. The exceptions are clear: deadline 까지 (모레까지) and subject 가 (모레가 토요일이에요) do attach. Don't confuse 모레 with 내일 (only one day off) or stretch it to mean any vague 'in a couple of days' — it is exactly the day after tomorrow.
